title: Ruling cards and five-point scale
subject: Islamic Studies
source: Seeded from islamic-studies/y8 lesson 9 (Pupil PDF worksheet: ruling cards and five-point scale)
intro: Lesson 9: Halal, haram and the five rulings. To understand the five rulings scholars use to classify every action, and why the default in everyday things is permissible

blocks.title: Sort into: Fard / Mustahabb / Mubah / Makruh
blocks.task: sort them into the columns: Fard, Mustahabb, Mubah, Makruh.
blocks.answer: Fard: The five daily prayers; Fasting Ramadan. Mustahabb: Siwak; Smiling at a Muslim. Mubah: Eating an apple. Makruh: Wasting water in wudu

cards:
fard / wajib (فَرْض / وَاجِب)
obligatory: rewarded if done,
sin if left

mustahabb (مُسْتَحَبّ)
recommended: rewarded if done,
no sin if left

mubah (مُبَاح)
permissible: neither reward
nor sin in itself

makruh (مَكْرُوه)
disliked: rewarded if left, no
sin if done

haram (حَرَام)
forbidden: sin if done,
rewarded if left for Allah
blocks.task: use them to test yourself or a partner.

questions.q: Explain the difference between makruh and haram.
questions.a: Haram brings sin if done; makruh does not bring sin, but leaving it is rewarded.
questions.model: Point: both are things to avoid, but differ in weight. Explain: haram is sinful if done; makruh is disliked, so a Muslim gains reward by leaving it but is not sinful if he does it. Example: wasting water in wudu is disliked.

questions.q: Ruling cards on the pupil PDF: place twelve everyday actions on the five-point scale and justify four of them in the portal response box with evidence where known. Start: '... is ... because ...'
questions.a: Correct placements, for example backbiting haram (49:12), sadaqah mustahabb, sleeping mubah, Ramadan fard
questions.model: Teacher places 'backbiting': 'Haram, because Allah forbids it in al-Hujurat 49:12.'

questions.q: how can a mubah action become rewarded?
questions.a: With a good intention, such as eating to be strong for worship

questions.q: Which ruling: rewarded if done, sin if left?
Back to our ponder: is everything not mentioned forbidden?
questions.a: No: everyday things are allowed unless evidence forbids
